name: Alternate-day fasting
lead: Alternate-day fasting (ADF) is an intermittent fasting pattern in which fast days alternate with unrestricted "feast" days. In the strict form no calories are eaten on fast days; in the modified form roughly a quarter of usual energy needs, often 0 to 500 kcal, is allowed.[1][2]

People use it to lose body fat and get leaner, which changes how the face and body look: less body fat shows sharper facial structure, a more visible jawline and more muscle definition. Practitioners describe it as a way to reach and hold a lean physique without counting calories every day, since the rule is about which days to eat rather than what to weigh out.[2][3]

Randomized trials in adults with obesity and in healthy non-obese people have compared ADF with daily calorie restriction or normal eating. Reviews describe it as producing clinically meaningful weight loss that is generally comparable to continuous calorie restriction, and a 2025 network meta-analysis of 99 trials found ADF the one fasting pattern with a modest weight-loss edge over continuous restriction.[1][2][3][12][13] A 2021 trial in lean adults found that fasting-day patterns matter less than total energy intake for fat loss.[17]

ADF sits within the wider intermittent fasting trend, which was reported as the most popular diet in the United States in 2018 and which spread through media, biohacking circles and fitness communities.[1]
infobox: About 2.5 to 9.9% in human studies, mostly fat[1]

paras: Alternate-day fasting is one of the most studied forms of intermittent fasting, alongside the 5:2 diet and time-restricted eating.[2] Wikipedia defines it as alternating a 24-hour fast day with under 25 percent of usual energy needs and a normal feast day; complete ADF allows no calories on fast days, whereas modified ADF allows up to a quarter of daily needs.[1] In trials, fast-day intake of 0 to 500 kcal is typical.[2]

Other intermittent patterns differ in timing. The 5:2 diet uses about 500 to 600 calories on two non-consecutive days of the week with normal eating on the other five; time-restricted eating confines food to a daily window of roughly 8 to 12 hours; periodic or whole-day fasting uses water-only fasts of 24 hours or more.[1][14] The 5:2 diet was first documented in a 2011 article co-authored by Michelle Harvie and Mark Mattson and was popularised in the UK and Australia by Michael Mosley's 2012 BBC Horizon documentary, Eat, Fast and Live Longer, which he made after learning about the approach from Mattson.[1][28]

Researchers describe a physiological rationale in which, after the fast day's stored glucose is used up, the body shifts toward fat-derived fuel such as ketones. Reviews list this metabolic switching, together with a large weekly energy deficit, as the pathway to weight and fat loss.[4][22] Across ADF, 5:2 and time-restricted eating, reviews report reductions in energy intake of 10 to 30 percent from baseline.[14]

Therapeutic fasts for obesity have been studied since at least 1915, with renewed medical interest in the 1960s after an enthusiastic report by Bloom and colleagues. Early studies used fasts of 1 to 14 days. Popular magazines picked up the idea, and by 1963 and 1964 clinicians were publishing cautions against unmonitored fasting.[1]

Alternate-day regimens were examined in animals and then humans. A 2003 PNAS study of mice found that alternate-day feeding improved glucose metabolism and neuronal resistance to injury without reducing overall food intake.[11] A 2005 study in non-obese adults examined body weight, body composition and energy metabolism under ADF,[6] and a 2007 review summarised human and animal trials on chronic disease prevention.[19] Short-term modified ADF in obese adults was reported in 2009,[7] and a 12-week trial in normal-weight and overweight adults followed in 2013.[5]

The 2010s brought the diet to mass audiences. The 5:2 diet reached the public through Mosley's 2012 documentary, and the US-based International Food Information Council reported in 2018 that intermittent fasting was the most popular diet in a national survey.[1][28] Mark Mattson, a neuroscientist and leading fasting researcher, summarised the field for general readers in The Intermittent Fasting Revolution (MIT Press, 2022).[1]

Practitioners choose a strict version with no calories on fast days or a modified version that allows a small meal; eating on feast days is typically unrestricted. Combination with exercise is common: a trial in obese adults combined ADF with endurance exercise,[9] and another combined ADF with aerobic exercise in people with fatty liver disease.[15] Many people describe doing ADF for a limited period, and trials generally run from weeks to a year.[3][20]

A 2022 review in Nature Reviews Endocrinology states that intermittent fasting diets can produce clinically significant weight loss.[2] Wikipedia summarises most human studies as showing weight loss of about 2.5 to 9.9 percent, mostly fat, with some lean mass lost, and limited evidence of superiority over continuous calorie restriction.[1] An Annual Review of Nutrition summary reports mild to moderate weight loss of 1 to 8 percent and 10 to 30 percent reductions in energy intake across ADF, 5:2 and time-restricted eating.[14] A Spanish-language review concluded that most studies show benefits on body composition, with weight loss and reduced fat mass, while cardiometabolic markers varied more.[23]

A 2023 meta-analysis of 24 randomized trials (1,768 participants) found intermittent fasting regimens gave similar weight loss to continuous energy restriction (mean difference 0.26 kg, 95% CI -0.31 to 0.84), with compliance above 80 percent in trials shorter than three months; in its exploratory ranking, ADF placed first, ahead of continuous restriction and time-restricted eating.[13]

A 2025 BMJ network meta-analysis of 99 randomised trials in 6,582 adults found that all intermittent fasting and continuous restriction diets produced more weight loss than eating freely. ADF was the only fasting approach to reduce weight more than continuous restriction, by about 1.3 kg (moderate certainty), and it also edged ahead of time-restricted eating and whole-day fasting. The authors report that differences between fasting and continuous restriction were minor overall, and that in trials of 24 weeks or longer only the advantage over unrestricted eating was clearly shown.[12]

A Canadian systematic review identified 27 weight-loss trials in overweight and obese people, mostly small and short (2 to 26 weeks); all found weight loss of 0.8 to 13.0 percent of baseline weight, and 12 studies comparing fasting with calorie restriction found equivalent results.[20] A 2025 randomised trial compared a ketogenic diet, time-restricted eating and ADF in adults with obesity.[18]

Reported short-term effects of intermittent fasting include hunger, irritability, dizziness, nausea, headaches and impaired thinking, typically fading within about a month. Dropout rates in a 2019 review ranged from 2 to 38 percent.[1] A trial of strict ADF in healthy middle-aged people reported no adverse effects, including at follow-up beyond six months.[4] A review concluded that intermittent fasting did not cause energy level disturbances or increased disordered eating in the studies it covered.[14] Wikipedia notes that fasting is not reported to improve athletic performance and that prolonged exercise after an overnight fast can be impaired.[1]

Intermittent fasting is not recommended for pregnant or breastfeeding women, children and adolescents, older adults, underweight people and those with or at risk of eating disorders. People with diabetes are advised to seek medical supervision.[1] The NHS advises people considering the 5:2 diet to consult a physician first, the US National Institute on Aging in 2018 did not recommend it for the general public, and a 2021 American Heart Association statement described the evidence for popular diets including intermittent fasting as insufficient for heart-health promotion.[1][28] A 2023 Cell Metabolism study reported that sustained alternate-day fasting potentiated doxorubicin cardiotoxicity, a finding relevant to people receiving chemotherapy, and a companion commentary discussed the same result.[16][26]

A 2017 JAMA Internal Medicine randomized trial compared ADF with daily calorie restriction and a no-intervention control in 100 metabolically healthy adults with obesity (mean BMI 34) over a 6-month weight-loss phase and a 6-month maintenance phase. It was described as the first long-term randomized trial of ADF. Weight loss was similar between the two diet groups at 6 and 12 months; the ADF group had the highest dropout rate (38 percent), and HDL cholesterol rose at 6 months while LDL was higher at 12 months in the ADF group. The authors concluded ADF was not better than daily restriction for adherence, weight loss, maintenance or cardioprotection.[3]

A 2019 randomized trial in healthy non-obese adults found that four weeks of strict ADF, with an average 37 percent calorie reduction, improved markers of general health including cardiovascular markers, with no adverse effects even after more than six months.[4] A 12-week trial of 32 normal-weight and overweight adults compared an ADF group, whose fast day allowed 25 percent of energy, with controls.[5] Earlier work examined nonobese subjects,[6] short-term modified ADF in obese adults,[7] zero-calorie ADF versus daily restriction in obesity,[8] and ADF combined with endurance exercise.[9]

A 2021 Science Translational Medicine trial in 36 healthy lean adults ran three weeks with three arms: alternate-day fasting with 150 percent of needs on eating days, a daily 25 percent restriction, and alternate-day fasting with 200 percent intake so there was no net restriction. Daily restriction produced the largest weight loss (about 1.9 kg), fasting with restriction about 1.6 kg, and fasting without net restriction about 0.5 kg; fat loss was about 1.8 kg, 0.7 kg and 0.1 kg respectively. The authors interpret this as showing that fat loss tracked energy deficit rather than fasting itself.[17]

A 2023 Cell Metabolism randomized trial in 80 adults with obesity and fatty liver disease (81 percent women) compared ADF with a 600 kcal fast day combined with exercise, either alone, and a control over three months.[15] A 2015 review examined body composition and clinical health markers.[10] A 2022 randomized trial in a nursing journal tested intermittent fasting for weight loss and cardiometabolic risk reduction.[25]

Intermittent fasting has become a mainstream diet fad with celebrity endorsement, and companies have sold coaching, supplements and meal packages around it; Wikipedia reports criticism of unsupported claims and describes the trend as having started in Silicon Valley biohacking.[1] ADF is the heavier-restriction end of that scene, often compared in forums with the 5:2 diet and with eating windows.

In fitness, bodybuilding and appearance settings the recurring question is muscle: people ask whether fasting costs lean mass. The cited human studies describe weight lost mostly as fat with some lean mass lost.[1] T Nation forum threads have cited the 2007 ADF review while discussing meal timing for lean physiques,[27] and a 2021 Hacker News thread discussed alternate-day fasting versus calorie restriction for fat loss in lean adults, with a further 2025 thread on ADF versus time-restricted eating in non-obese people.[21][24]
In the 2003 study, mice on an alternate-day regimen showed improved glucose metabolism and neuronal resistance to injury without a reduction in overall food intake.[11]

lore.intro: ADF is discussed in fitness, bodybuilding and technical forums as a way to get lean, usually alongside questions about muscle retention and how it compares with other diets.[21][27]

claims.claim: Fasting every other day is an easy route to a lean face and body.
claims.believers: Proponents say a simple rule of eating normally one day and little the next removes daily calorie counting and produces visible fat loss.
claims.experts: Reviews report clinically meaningful weight loss, mostly fat, comparable to daily restriction, with dropout in some trials as high as 38 percent.[3][13]

claims.claim: ADF beats ordinary calorie cutting for fat loss.
claims.believers: Some followers hold that the alternating pattern has a special metabolic edge over steady dieting.
claims.experts: The 2025 BMJ network meta-analysis found ADF about 1.3 kg ahead of continuous restriction in shorter trials, while the 2017 JAMA trial and the 2023 meta-analysis found comparable results and a 2021 lean-adult trial found energy deficit explained the fat loss.[3][12][13][17]

claims.claim: Fasting days burn fat while sparing muscle.
claims.believers: Practitioners say fasting shifts the body toward fat and ketone fuel and that lean mass is largely preserved.
claims.experts: Wikipedia's summary says human studies show mostly fat loss with some lean mass lost.[1][4]

claims.claim: Fasting itself, apart from calories, drives health benefits.
claims.believers: Followers cite animal studies in which alternate-day feeding improved glucose handling without lowering total intake.[11]
claims.experts: In the 2021 lean-adult trial, fasting without net energy restriction produced little weight or fat change and no fasting-specific metabolic benefit was reported.[17]

claims.claim: ADF is safe for anyone who wants to try it.
claims.believers: Users describe hunger and low energy that fade after the first weeks.
claims.experts: Reviews report no serious adverse events in most trials, while guidance advises against it in pregnancy, adolescence, underweight and eating-disorder histories, and a 2023 study linked sustained ADF to worse doxorubicin cardiotoxicity.[1][14][16][20]

claims.claim: ADF can be combined with training to build a better physique.
claims.believers: Lifters discuss pairing fast days with endurance or resistance work.
claims.experts: Trials have combined ADF with endurance exercise and aerobic exercise, reporting weight and liver-fat outcomes; Wikipedia states fasting does not appear to improve athletic performance.[1][9][15]

card.summary: Fast every other day; trials show weight loss, but not clearly more than ordinary calorie cutting.
card.note: Not advised for pregnancy, adolescents, or people with eating-disorder histories.

quick.overview:
Alternate-day fasting alternates fast days (no or very few calories) with normal eating days. It is used for fat loss.

Randomized trials report meaningful weight loss and some improved health markers, with results generally comparable to daily calorie restriction.
quick.mechanism: The fast days create a large weekly calorie deficit; researchers also study metabolic switching and hormone changes.
quick.risks: Hunger, irritability, headaches and low energy are reported early on. It is advised against in pregnancy, youth, underweight people and those with eating disorders.

chain: Alternating very-low-energy days with normal days
Fat loss, leaner face and body
angle.text: ADF reduces weekly energy intake by cutting calories sharply every second day, which leads to weight loss that is mostly fat. A leaner face and body is the appearance payoff proponents describe; trials report weight loss in the same range as daily calorie restriction.
